analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion education-law changes entirely.
analysis.headline: The full-repeal bill never advanced past its initial committee referral; no vote was ever taken on it in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 as of January 1, 2018, and put the pre-2010 rules back in place [S2][S3]. That means the end of Medicaid expansion, marketplace subsidies, protections for people with pre-existing conditions, required coverage of preventive care, and a series of taxes on high earners and health-related industries. It would also undo the 2010 change that cut private banks out of federal student lending, sending those loans back through bank middlemen [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest gains would go to high-income households, who would stop paying the ACA's 3.8% tax on investment income and the extra Medicare payroll tax on wages above $200,000/$250,000. Medical device makers, brand-name drug makers, health insurers, and tanning businesses would be freed from ACA fees and rules. Banks and student-loan companies would re-enter federal student lending as middlemen, a business the 2010 law ended.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, device and drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act entirely, effective January 1, 2018, and restores the laws it changed as if it had never passed [S3].

Also repeals the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, which alongside the ACA ended bank-based federal student lending and redirected savings to Pell Grants and deficit reduction [S3].
The bill sets its own pay-as-you-go budget accounting, using a statement prepared by the House Budget chairman rather than the standard scoring process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of people who gained coverage or protections under the ACA would bear the cost: Medicaid expansion enrollees, marketplace subsidy recipients, people with pre-existing conditions who would again face denial or surcharges, seniors paying the prescription-drug coverage gap, and students whose Pell Grant funding came from the repealed law's savings.
analysis.who_pays_short: ACA coverage recipients and student aid recipients

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ACA would remove the Medicaid expansion and marketplace subsidies that extended coverage to millions, the ban on denying or charging more to people with pre-existing conditions, and the requirement that plans cover preventive care and dependents up to age 26 — all of which the bill would erase without a replacement [S2][S3].

Restoring the 2010 status quo on student loans would again route federal student loans through private lenders, reintroducing the intermediary costs the 2010 law eliminated, and would claw back the Pell Grant funding that law created [S3].

The bill includes no replacement financing for any ACA provisions and relies on a pay-as-you-go statement prepared by the House Budget chairman, letting its own passage sidestep the standard budget scoring process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concentrated and the losses are broad: tax relief for high earners and fee relief for health-related industries on one side, versus the loss of coverage, subsidies, and consumer protections relied on by millions of people, with nothing offered to replace them. As written, the bill's costs to ordinary households outweigh its benefits.

outcome.mechanism: Cruz introduced it with three cosponsors on January 12, 2017; the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the ObamaCare Repeal Act on January 12, 2017, with Senators Mike Lee, Marco Rubio, and Rand Paul as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it never received a vote in either chamber during the 115th Congress [S5].
The bill's total text is two repeal sections and a pay-as-you-go accounting provision; it offered no replacement for the laws it would erase [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the ACA's coverage expansions, pre-existing-condition protections, and student-aid funding stayed in place, so the people who rely on them were better off than under the bill. The ACA's taxes on high earners and health industries also remained on the books.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on ACA protections

for.name: Sens. Mike Lee, Marco Rubio, and Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the full-repeal bill; all three cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it, held no markup, and never scheduled a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had four Republican sponsors and cosponsors and no Democratic support on record; it never reached a roll call, so there was no vote breakdown.

industries.note: Repeal would erase the ACA's 3.8% tax on investment income and the additional Medicare payroll tax on high wages — tax cuts that flow mainly to the wealthiest households and are paid for by repealing coverage subsidies ordinary people use.

Repeal frees insurers from ACA coverage rules, rate reviews, and fees, but also takes away the subsidized marketplace customers and mandate that guaranteed them volume. Deregulation would come at the direct expense of the protections policyholders rely on.
Repeal would eliminate the ACA's tax on medical device sales, a cost relief the industry lobbied for; the offsetting revenue had helped fund coverage expansion.
Repeal would end the ACA's annual fee on branded prescription drugs and close the Medicare coverage gap that caps seniors' drug costs, shifting costs back to beneficiaries.

Repealing the 2010 reconciliation act would restore bank-based federal student lending, putting private lenders back in the middle of the program as paid intermediaries and cutting the Pell Grant funding that law created.
